First-Ever Supercharged Shelby Mustang GT350R Needs a New Owner, No Other Like It Exists
46 photos
Photo: YouTube/Lou Costabile
Typically, when a car wears an “R” in its nameplate but only on certain, select versions, it means it’s in a huRRy. It’s Rapid. Its motor puts out more poweR and toRque, it acceleRates quickeR, and hits higher top speeds, therefore it’s fasteR. In other words, it’s like a Race car, but Road legal. Which is gReat – for those who have one. Pete Wojtowicz has one, and it only needs a drop or two or Red to be the greatest All-American pony car ever.
If you spend enough time talking cars with Mustang guys, the Shelby GT350R always comes up with a certain grin. Back in 1965, Carroll Shelby took a simple Ford fastback and turned it into a proper track bully. The regular K-code street version was already plenty quick , but that extra R meant pure business, giving weekend racers a stripped, loud, high-winding V8 machine built to embarrass much pricier European sports cars.
Across four generations, that basic recipe never really changed. You bought the standard Shelby when you wanted a factory warranty and a fun Sunday cruiser, and you stepped up to the R when you only cared about going fast. Because production numbers stayed tiny in every era, spotting one on the street is rare. Recently, though, a really wild sleeper popped up near Indianapolis, courtesy of Lou Costabile, the classic car YouTuber who documented it on camera.
It’s a 2011 Ford Mustang Shelby GT350R owned by Pete Wojtowicz (if the name doesn’t sound familiar, I’ll have you know he also owns a 1-in-12 Shelby Mustang GT350H in Red with gold stripes, and a 2024 Shelby Series II – the first one ever built).
Photo: YouTube/Lou Costabile At first glance, his 2011 GT350R looks like a clean throwback to 1965, finished in white with painted blue stripes, blue mirrors, a smooth nose, and blocked quarter windows carrying Carroll Shelby’s autograph. Under the scooped hood sits a 5.0-liter V8 with a Ford Racing Whipple supercharger.
Standard supercharged 2011 GT350 builds made 525 horsepower, while ordering the R race tune pushed output to 625 horsepower, and this particular car actually put down 650 horsepower on the dyno. It runs a McLeod dual-plate clutch, a short-throw 6-speed manual shifter, and a one-piece aluminum driveshaft. Shelby brakes, pillar gauges, sequential taillights, and a screaming center exit exhaust make it an absolute riot on pavement.
The backstory on this Mustang is where things get really good. It was the second to last example of the first 20 VIP cars reserved by Shelby American executive Gary Patterson strictly for employees and close friends. Folks call this batch the “Encore Series” because 2011 was the last Shelby GT350 model Carroll Shelby gave his blessing to. Its first owner was Warren Faris, a high-ranking official at Shelby American back then.
Photo: YouTube/Lou Costabile When the bosses of Ford Racing and Special Vehicle Technologies heard Warren was getting the first R upgrade, they made custom GT350R door sills just for him. Every other 2011 GT350R was left unbadged, needing paperwork or a dyno run to prove what it was. That, and the fact that is puts down more horsepower than all that came in its wake, makes this spectacular GT350R a one-off.
After passing on $100,000 MSRPs in 2011, Pete found this gem in Fort Myers, Florida, 3 years ago. The bigger Shelby Mustang story started in 1965 when Ford boss Lee Iacocca asked Carroll Shelby to build a Corvette fighter, before adding the big block GT500 in 1967. First generation GT350 production ran from 1965 to 1970, opening with 562 cars in 1965, including 36 factory GT350R racers. Their 289 cubic-inch V8 packed 306 horsepower, or 350 horsepower in R spec, backed by a 4-speed manual.
Those early cars earned their reputation on the track right away. Ken Miles drove GT350R prototype 5R002 to victory in Texas in February 1965, kicking off three straight SCCA B Production championships from 1965 through 1967. When new, base prices ran at $5,950 for the 1965 Shelby Mustang GT350R. Prototype 5R002 fetched a record $3,850,000 at a Mecum auction in 2020 – the highest price of any Mustang ever sold publicly.
Photo: YouTube/Lou Costabile After a 46-year break, Shelby American revived the name from 2011 to 2013, converting 159 Mustangs in 2011, 132 in 2012, and 36 in 2013. Buyers paired 6-speed manual or automatic transmissions with a 5.0-liter V8 (the first-generation Coyote legend) making 525 in standard GT350 guise or 625 horsepower and 575 lb-ft (780 Nm) in the 80 R-rated, steroid-fed examples.
It wasn’t a standalone model , but a post-title upgrade on an existing Mustang GT, with the upgrade costing a whopping $33,995. For reference, note that the standard donor vehicle started at $30,890. With other Shelby add-ons, a new car left the assembly line with an ear tag of $83,000 or more.
Ford took over from 2015 to 2020, building 3,647 track-focused GT350R model, with a 5.2-liter flat-plane crank V8 (the nefarious naturally aspirated “Voodoo” powerhouse) delivering 526 horsepower and 429 lb-ft (582 Nm) through a Tremec 6-speed manual. The GT350R-C won the 2016 IMSA championship.
Photo: YouTube/Lou Costabile For 2025 and 2026, Shelby American returned on the S650 chassis, capping yearly builds at 562 GT350s and 36 GT350R track brawlers alongside a Trans Am racer. Its Whipple supercharged 5.0-liter V8 Coyote pairs with 6-speed manuals or 10-speed automatic gearboxes to make 830 horsepower in R trim.
This 15-year-fresh example isn’t afraid to put some wrinkles on the tarmac, as Pete joyously feathers the throttle just enough to make rear-wheel grip scream for mercy. He’s not overdoing it, though, nbut even the slightest touch of the l oud pedal pushes the occupants deep in the seats – watch the end of the video to see how the owner gave Lou a big smile with nothing but torque and supercharger whine. Oh, and by the way, if you like this car more than a lot, ask Lou for Pete’s details – it is for sale.
